Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction: Fever, jaundice, falling Hb 3‑14 days, positive indirect Coombs, no acute renal signs — Mild – asymptomatic fall in Hb; Moderate – symptomatic anemia, jaundice; Severe – renal impairment, severe anemia.

qs.q: A patient experiences an unexpected drop in hemoglobin and mild jaundice approximately 7 days after receiving a blood transfusion. A direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is positive. Which blood group system is most notoriously associated with this type of delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction?
qs.e: The Kidd blood group system (Jka, Jkb antigens) is notoriously associated with delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions. Antibodies to Kidd antigens (anti-Jka, anti-Jkb) are often weak or undetectable in pre-transfusion testing but can rapidly increase after re-exposure, leading to extravascular hemolysis typically 3-10 days post-transfusion.

qs.q: Which blood group system is most frequently associated with delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions that present with a rapid drop in hemoglobin but negative initial antibody screens?
qs.e: The Kidd system is the classic cause of delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions. Antibodies fade quickly, screen negative, then surge after re-exposure causing rapid intravascular hemolysis.

exam: What is the most likely cause of a patient who develops fever and jaundice 5 days after a blood transfusion? — Alloimmunisation to a minor red cell antigen; look for a positive indirect Coombs.

How would you differentiate delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction from acute hemolytic transfusion reaction? — Timing (days vs minutes), intravascular vs extravascular hemolysis, and Coombs positivity.
A patient with DHTR develops acute kidney injury. What is the most appropriate next step? — Initiate renal replacement therapy and consider exchange transfusion.
Why are steroids used in the treatment of DHTR? — They suppress antibody production and reduce hemolysis.
What laboratory test is essential when DHTR is suspected but the hospital lacks a Coombs kit? — A simple CBC with reticulocyte count and bilirubin to assess hemolysis.

In a low‑resource setting, a patient with suspected DHTR shows a falling Hb but no fever. What should you do? — Continue monitoring Hb, bilirubin and renal function; consider exchange transfusion if Hb falls below 7 g/dL.
ai.title: Delayed Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A late immune reaction to transfused red cells, presenting 3‑14 days after transfusion with fever, jaundice and a falling haemoglobin. Diagnosis relies on a positive indirect Coombs test and clinical context.

sections.p: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR) is an immune-mediated destruction of transfused erythrocytes that becomes apparent days after the transfusion. It is distinguished from acute reactions by its timing and the predominance of extravascular hemolysis.

t.b: Detects antibodies against transfused red cells; a positive result confirms immune hemolysis
Elevated indirect bilirubin indicates hemolysis; a rise >2 mg/dL is significant
A fall >2 g/dL from baseline suggests hemolysis
Elevated reticulocytes (>3%) support marrow response to anemia

b: Moderate – symptomatic anemia, jaundice, Hb drop 2–4 g/dL
Severe – severe anemia, renal impairment, Hb drop >4 g/dL
sections.p: Severity is graded by haemoglobin drop, clinical symptoms and organ involvement. The WHO‑based scale is useful in low‑resource settings.

b: Alloimmunisation to Rh, Kell, Duffy, Kidd
sections.p: The leading cause is alloimmunisation to red cell antigens, often to minor antigens not routinely typed. Other causes include autoantibodies and infections that alter antigen expression.

t.b: Identifies mismatched antigens; absence of typing increases risk

sections.p: Patients develop fever, chills, back pain, jaundice and a gradual drop in haemoglobin. Renal dysfunction may appear late.

t.b: Checks for hemoglobinuria; usually negative in DHTR

sections.p: Key tests confirm hemolysis and rule out other causes. In resource‑poor settings, a simple CBC, bilirubin and indirect Coombs are essential.
Severe anemia, acute kidney injury, shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation are life‑threatening complications.

t.b: Prolonged PT/INR or aPTT indicates DIC

sections.p: Immediate cessation of transfusion, supportive care and immunosuppression. In low‑resource settings, steroids and exchange transfusion are mainstays.

Removes alloantibodies and replaces with antigen‑matched blood

Use antigen‑matched blood for future transfusions
sections.p: Monitor haemoglobin, bilirubin and renal function for 2 weeks. Future transfusions require extended antigen typing and avoidance of repeated exposure.
